decisions.note: Signals to review: packing a strong hand costs wins, and staying with a weak one is sometimes a deliberate bluff.

limitations: Card strength assumes every opponent stays to the end against a random hand. Real opponents pack weak hands, so a strong hand is worth somewhat less than shown.
Variants with jokers, table cards or discards have no card-only strength model and are left out.
A hand’s value uses the pot that was actually played, which depends a little on how everyone bet, including you.
Packing a weak hand is usually right and counts as good play here. "Play" still mixes skill, bluffing, reading opponents and their luck; it is not a pure skill score.
Strength is each starting hand’s heads-up equity against a random hand, scaled to the table size. It ignores position, stacks and everything after the flop.
Pot-odds checks apply only to heads-up preflop decisions and compare against a random hand, which flatters weak hands against a raiser.
The decision counts are signals to review, not a mistake rate.
Exact for this table’s rules (no splits, dealer stands on 17, no peek) assuming an infinite deck. A real single deck changes values by a small amount.
Only hit, stand and double are evaluated; a timed-out turn is automatic and not counted.
Expected results use the best play from each starting hand; the gap to your actual result is luck plus the cost of any mistakes.

method.cards: What your cards were worth: if everyone stayed to the end, each hand’s win chance times its pot, minus its fair share. Zero for an average deal.
method.play: What you did beyond the cards: what you actually won or lost minus what those cards were worth. Packing a hand that was worth less than nothing counts in your favour. Mixes skill, bluffing and opponents’ luck.
method.outcome: What happened: boots won or lost. Always cards + play.
method.exact: Solved for this game’s rules, no estimation involved.
method.estimated: A model with stated assumptions; read as a range.

what: Every hand’s deck is shuffled and sealed on the server before anyone sees a card. The seal is a fingerprint that is published with the hand, so the deck cannot be swapped afterwards.
A player then chooses where the deck is cut, so the server alone cannot decide who gets which cards.
After the hand, the recorded game replays exactly from its own history, which checks the result matches the rules.
cannot: It cannot prove a shuffle was random in a single hand: any one deal is just one of many possible deals.
It cannot show deck order or the seal’s secret. Those stay private so a table could never be scouted.
A run of bad cards is normal. With dozens of cards, some ranks will always look a little busy.
explain.howToRead: Bars sit inside a 95% band when the deal looks like a fair one. Expect about one in twenty to poke outside by chance. We only call a deal unusual when several tests agree after correcting for how many things were checked.
